source_text: Γλώσσης δὲ φείδεσθαι καλόν, καὶ εὐσταθούσῃ χρῆσθαι καρδίᾳ ἐν τῇ περὶ λόγους σπουδῇ. Οὐ γὰρ χρὴ ἀλογίστως αὐτῶν ἔχοντα, κἂν ἄτοπα, ἢ τὰ ἐπὶ νοῦν ἐλθόντα, ταῦτα προΐεσθαι διὰ τῆς φωνῆς· ἀλλ᾽ ἐνθυμουμένους, ὅτι εἰ καὶ πολὺ ἀφεστήκαμεν οὐρανοῦ, γινώσκειν χρή, ὅτι ἐπ᾽ ἐπηκόῳ φθεγγόμεθα Θεοῦ, καὶ ἔστι λυσιτελὲς λαλεῖν ἀπεριπτώτως. Ὥσπερ δὲ φροντίσι ψυχῆς ποικίλαις παρέπεται ὀνειράτων παντοδαπῇ φαντασίᾳ· οὕτω καὶ ἀφροσύνῃ φλυαρία συνέζευκται. Ἐπαγγελία δὲ δι᾽ εὐχῆς γινομένη, τέλος λαμβανέτω δι᾽ ἔργου. Ἀφρόνων δὲ ἴδιον, τὸ ἀποβλήτους εἶναι· σὺ δὲ ἀληθὴς ἔσο, γινώσκων ὡς πολλῷ ἄμεινον μὴ εὔξασθαί σε, μηδὲ ὑποσχέσθαι τὶ δρᾶσαι, ἢ εὐξάμενον, εἶτα παραλιπεῖν. Δεῖ δὲ παντοίως φεύγειν τὴν τῶνδε καλῶν ῥημάτων ἐπιρροήν, ὡς ἀκουσομένου θεοῦ. Τῷ γὰρ ταῦτα ἐνθυμουμένῳ πλέον οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἢ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι τῶν ἑαυτοῦ ἔργων ὑπὸ θεοῦ διαφθειρομένων. Ὥσπερ γὰρ τὰ πολλὰ ἐνύπνια μάταια, οὕτω καὶ τὰ πολλὰ ῥήματα. Φόβος δὲ Θεοῦ, ἀνθρώπων σωτήριος, σπάνιος δέ. Ὅθεν οὐ χρὴ θαυμάζειν ἀφορῶντα πρός τε πένητας συκοφαντουμένους, καὶ πρὸς δικαστὰς παραλογιζομένους. Χρὴ δὲ ἐκτρέπεσθαι τὸ τῶν δυνατωτέρων μείζονας εἶναι δοκεῖν. Κἂν γὰρ ἐκγένηται τοῦτο, ἀλλ᾽ οὖν τῶν ἐσομένων σοι φοβερῶν, οὐ ῥύσεταί σε ἡ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν πονηρία.
thought_title: Guard the tongue and keep your vows
orientation: Guard the tongue, keep your vows and fear God, for many words are as empty as dreams.
pass_a_gloss: It is good to spare the tongue, and to use a steady heart in the zeal about words. For one ought not, holding toward them unreasoningly, to send forth through the voice even absurd things, or the things that have come to mind; but, considering, one ought to know that, even if we stand far off from heaven, we utter within the hearing of God, and it is profitable to speak without falling, without blunder. And just as to varied cares of the soul there attends an all-kinds imagination of dreams, so also to folly babble has been yoked together. And a promise coming about through a vow, prayer, let it take its completion through deed. And it is the property of the senseless to be rejected, cast away; but you be true, knowing that it is much better for you not to vow, nor to promise to do anything, than, having vowed, then to leave it aside. And one must in every way flee the influx, flood of these fine words, as God being about to hear. For to the one considering these things there is nothing more than to perceive his own works being destroyed by God. For as the many dreams are vain, so also the many words. And the fear of God is saving for men, but rare. Whence one ought not to wonder, looking off toward both poor men being oppressed and toward judges reasoning falsely. And one ought to turn away from the seeming to be greater than the more powerful. For even if this should come about, be possible, yet from the fearful things that will be for you, the wickedness by itself will not rescue you.

pass_b_english: It is good to spare the tongue, and to keep a steady heart in your eagerness to speak (Ecclesiastes 5:2). For we must not be careless about our words and let slip through the voice whatever comes into the mind, even when it is out of place. Rather, we must bear in mind that, though we stand far from heaven, we speak within God's hearing (Ecclesiastes 5:2), and that it pays to speak without stumbling. Just as all manner of dream images attend the varied cares of the soul, so idle chatter is yoked to folly (Ecclesiastes 5:3).

A promise made by a vow should be fulfilled in deed (Ecclesiastes 5:4). It is the mark of fools to be cast aside (Ecclesiastes 5:4); but you, be truthful, knowing that it is far better for you not to vow, and not to promise to do anything, than to vow and then leave it undone (Ecclesiastes 5:5). You must flee by every means the flood of such fine-sounding words, knowing that God will hear them (Ecclesiastes 5:6). For the one who sets his mind on such things gains nothing but to watch his own works being destroyed by God (Ecclesiastes 5:6). For as many dreams are empty, so too are many words (Ecclesiastes 5:7). The fear of God brings salvation to human beings, but it is rare (Ecclesiastes 5:7).

So there is no need to wonder when you look at the poor being oppressed and at judges who reason dishonestly (Ecclesiastes 5:8). But you must avoid seeming to be greater than those who are more powerful (Ecclesiastes 5:8). For even if you should manage this, still wickedness, of itself, will not rescue you from the terrors that are to come upon you.
notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 5:2-9 in English numbering. Gregory's chapter 5 follows the LXX/Hebrew verse division, so LXX 5:1-8 = English 5:2-9; all citations use the English numbers. θεοῦ is lower case in the print at 'God will hear them' and 'destroyed by God' but plainly means God, so it is capitalised in English. οὐ in 'there is no need to wonder' is printed as text following the Opera omnia print (the transcription bracketed it as a supplement); the Latin 'nihil est cur mireris' agrees. In the dream comparison the Greek has two datives (φροντίσι ... φαντασίᾳ) with παρέπεται; read as 'dream images attend the cares of the soul'. κἂν ἄτοπα, ἢ τὰ ἐπὶ νοῦν ἐλθόντα is read as one idea, 'whatever comes into the mind, even when it is out of place'. 'Fine-sounding words' renders τῶνδε καλῶν ῥημάτων, taken as rash vows and boasts. 'Avoid seeming to be greater than those who are more powerful' takes τὸ ... δοκεῖν with the reader as subject; 'avoid thinking that the more powerful are greater' is a less likely reading. The last sentence ('your wickedness of itself will not rescue you') has no clear match in Ecclesiastes 5:9 ('the profit of the land is for all; the king is served by the field') and is left uncited.
